genius-80.preamble: Down solutions must be suitably 14 in order to be 17, not briefly edited, before being inserted in the grid. Three across clues have solutions that are 17 and are not further defined.
genius-80.source: https://fifteensquared.net/2010/02/28/guardian-genius-80-february-2010-puck/ (quotes the preamble; its bracketed glosses left out)

genius-81.preamble: Solutions are divided into four groups of seven. Each member of that group begins with the same letter. The definition in all 28 of these clues is normal (and is placed at the correct clue number), but all subsidiary parts of these clues have been swapped around. The correct subsidiary part for any definition can always be found in another clue where the solution begins with the same letter. All 28 subsidiary parts of these clues ignore the initial letter of the solution. The four letters that begin the solutions may be arranged to give something to drive.

genius-93.preamble: Seven clues require ill-advised exchanges before solutions are entered in the grid. The resulting solutions are non-words. In these seven clues, the definitions (indicated by the letter counts) are pre-operative and the cryptic parts are post-operative. All other clues are normal.
genius-93.source: https://fifteensquared.net/2011/04/03/guardian-genius-93-by-paul/ ("In the preamble we were told that")

genius-99.preamble: Each clue, presented in the form of a 10, contains a definition and a jumble of the letters of the solution. The jumble always starts at the start or ends at the end of a word in the clue. Seven of these jumbles contain one superfluous letter. These lead in clue order to the puzzle's theme.

genius-100.preamble: The spelling of several well-known (but undefined) entries is incorrect, which may not be to your taste!

genius-105.preamble: Seventeen clues lack a definition and lead to a partner in a well-known pairing. The required grid entry, however, is the other partner in the pairing. With these clues the letter count indicates the solution to the clue, not the word to be entered in the grid.

genius-115.preamble: Ten solutions can also be 30, initially. Any secondary definition or wordplay in their clues leads to the solution as it might appear if it were, indeed, 30 of any 26 12 before 22 down 22 across. With one of these cases, where proverbially the solution cannot be 30, a palatable alternative (carrying the smallest possible 26 14) is required.
genius-115.source: https://fifteensquared.net/2013/02/03/guardian-genius-no-115-by-puck/ ("The preamble read as follows"; numerals are clue references)

genius-117.preamble: Seven clues contain anagrams of their definitions for their solutions. Eight more clues have had their definitions removed and added, superfluously, to eight different clues. The remaining seven clues have had their definitions shuffled randomly.

genius-129.preamble: Eleven clues lead to the second part of a thematically related solution, not further defined. However, the letter counts with these clues refer to the first part of each of these solutions, which is to be entered in the grid.

genius-135.preamble: All solutions are thematic, wholly or in part. All clues contain normal definitions but, with 18 of them, the wordplay ignores the thematic element.

azed-2688.preamble: Nine across and nine down clues lead in their definitions to Spoonerisms of the correct answers to be entered. Subsidiary indications in these clues lead to the correct answers themselves. In the remaining clues (except 16) the definitions have been distorted by one Spoonerism per clue. Subsidiary indications in these clues likewise lead to the correct answers. Competitors should submit with their solutions a clue of the latter type to the asterisked definition at 16. NB Spoonerisms may be either consonantal, e.g. WHITEBAIT/BITE (or BIGHT) WAIT, or vocalic, e.g. BUNTING/BIN TONGUE, and may be accompanied by changes in punctuation. Bracketed numbers after clues indicate the length of grid entries throughout.
azed-2688.source: Guardian printable copy uploads.guim.co.uk/2023/12/21/AZ_2688_(24th_Dec).pdf (reader's overprint doubles removed)

azed-2655.preamble: Each clue, except 8, is a passage from which the printer has removed a hidden answer, closing the gap and sometimes taking liberties with the punctuation, but not disturbing the order of the remaining letters. Example: Vaulting above tunnel entrance appears inane, scary. Answer: PESTO. Undevilled version: Vaulting above tunnel entrance appears in an escape story. Every passage, when complete, makes reasonable sense. Competitors should submit with their entries a PD clue to replace the asterisked definition at 8. NB Preference is given to PD clues in which the break before and after the answer omitted (before and after omission) does not occur at the ends or beginnings of words in the clue. Please give the full undevilled version of your clue as well as the clue itself.
azed-2655.source: Guardian printable copy uploads.guim.co.uk/2023/05/06/AZ_2655_(07th_May).pdf (reader's overprint doubles removed)

azed-2595.preamble: Most of the entries contain one or two misprints, producing non-words. Every clue contains a definition of the un-misprinted entry and a subsidiary indication of the form entered. The misprints may be read to form a timely message. Competitors should submit with their entries a normal cryptic clue to the first two words of the message.
azed-2595.source: Guardian printable copy uploads.guim.co.uk/2022/03/05/AZ_2595_(06th_Mar).pdf (the anniversary lunch notice printed beside it left out)

azed-2566.preamble: In a Playfair word square the code phrase (in which no letter recurs) is followed by the remaining letters of the alphabet, I doing double duty for I and J. To encode a word it must first be split into pairs of letters, e.g. CR IT IC AL. Each pair is then to be seen as forming the diagonally opposite corners of a rectangle within the word square, the other two corners being the encoded form. Thus, in the example shown, CR gives SG (not GS, which RC would give). Where a pair of letters appears in the same row or column in the word square, its encoded form is produced from the letter immediately to the right of or below each respectively. For the last letter in a row or column the first letter in the same row or column becomes the encoded form. Thus IC becomes CE. When all the pairs are encoded, the word is joined up again, thus CRITICAL is encoded as SGCICEOP. The answers to the four asterisked clues, which are without definitions, must be encoded in the diagram. The code phrase (of two words, one of them an abbreviation) describes the answers to the asterisked clues. It must be deduced with the help of the answers to normal clues, so that the diagram may be completed.
azed-2566.source: Guardian printable copy uploads.guim.co.uk/2021/08/12/AZ_2566_(15th_Aug)_(1).pdf (read off the page image: the text layer starts mid-passage; the example square ORANG/ESTIC/KBDFH/LMPQU/VWXYZ is a graphic)

nation-3403.source: the puzzle's own 5-down clue states the theme (no preamble printed)

toughie-277.preamble: All answers contain at least one instance of the letters RE, which are ignored in the wordplay. The first number in brackets refers to the number of letters used in the wordplay.
toughie-277.source: https://bigdave44.com/2009/12/31/toughie-277/ (the blogger's hidden statement of the theme, which paraphrases Elgar's own instructions; the Telegraph's printed wording was not found; his aside that 10a is the exception left out)

azed-2040.preamble: Each clue, except 5, is a passage from which the printer has removed a hidden answer, closing the gap and sometimes taking liberties with the punctuation. Example: Vaulting above tunnel entrance appears inane, scary. Answer: PESTO. Undevilled version: Vaulting above tunnel entrance appears in an escape story. Every passage, when complete, makes reasonable sense. Competitors should submit with their solutions a 'PD' clue to replace the definition at 5. NB Preference is given to PD clues in which breaks before and after the word omitted (before and after omission) do not occur at the ends or beginnings of words in the clue. azed-2157.preamble: The symmetry of the bars in the completed diagram is such that it would look the same if turned upside down, but not if given a quarter turn. Clues are in their correct order. Competitors should mark bars in their solutions, but numbers are unnecessary. They should submit with their entries a normal cryptic clue to replace the definition asterisked.
azed-2157.source: Guardian printable copy of Azed 2,157 (andlit.org.uk); the text layer's run-together "entriesa" split

ftcryptic-14795.preamble: Sixteen solutions contain related groups, three reversed, which are ignored in the cryptic part of their clues
ftcryptic-14795.source: https://fifteensquared.net/2014/12/03/financial-times-14795-by-gozo/ (comment 3 quotes the printed instruction from the FT PDF)

genius-91.preamble: The 28 solutions are divided into four groups of seven, each member of a group beginning with the same letter. All 28 definitions are normal and positioned with the correct clue number, but the cryptic parts of the clues have been swapped around. The cryptic part for any definition will always be found in a clue whose solution begins with the same letter, though these ignore the initial letter of the solution.
genius-91.source: https://fifteensquared.net/2011/02/06/genius-91-by-tramp/ (comment #3 by JS quotes Tramp's special instructions in full)

nation-3391.source: the puzzle's own 28-across clue states the theme (no preamble printed; thenation.com/article/archive/puzzle-no-3391/)

listener-121.preamble: Diagonals (1 and 7). The softness of the first is due, ’tis reckoned, To overmuch attachment to the second.

listener-503.preamble: All solutions are words in the A.V. or R.V. text or margin including the Apocrypha.

listener-522.preamble: Each solution is a synonym of one or more words in the clue.

listener-941.preamble: Lights are to be entered in Morse—the International Code being used.

listener-985.preamble: Explanation. From one word, or from two or more consecutive words, in each clue take enough letters to leave the number stated in brackets at the end of the clue. The removed letters can be arranged to form a synonym of another word in the clue that may be inferred from the context; and the remaining letters are to be arranged as a word (the meaning of which is not indicated) to be entered on the diagram. For example, if the clue was ‘Pademelon with no skin (5)’, the letters PEEL (= skin) could be removed, leaving the letters ADMON, forming NOMAD, for entry on the diagram.

listener-1313.preamble: The clues lead to words which do not necessarily have the same number of letters as the corresponding lights. Before insertion in the diagram, figures must be substituted for any of the following Roman numerals (whether singly or in groups): I, V, X, L, C, D, M. The substituted figures are not necessarily the fewest possible from the Roman numerals which they replace. Thus, ALIVE might become A54E, A504E, A515E, or A5015E. The unchecked letters (taking all Is and Os to be figures) might be arranged to read: HURRY UP BERTS PATH. The sum of the digits in the complete diagram is 112. Punctuation is to be ignored.

listener-1526.preamble: Many moons have passed since the Djintecs contributed to this journal. Following another visit to this little-known South American race, Vectis has brought back a puzzle compiled by a Djintec family of father, mother, son and daughter (each of whom contributed exactly a quarter of the clues and lights). For the benefit of new readers, the Djintecs maintain a most high standard of education. However, although their children are now writing in the “orthodox” style, older generations still persist in using the ancient style of writing from right to left and from the bottom of the paper to the top. While this trait will be rectified in a generation or so, there can never be a change in the one characteristic peculiar to these peoples—from birth the male will say exactly what he means but the female will say just the opposite!

listener-1999.preamble: All the lights must be entered in two halves: the first half where the clue stands; the second elsewhere.

listener-2030.preamble: Because they regard it as a trifle, not worthy of consideration, critics, editors and biographers of Shakespeare never mention that he compiled a crossword (published here for the first time) or that he wrote the following extract from The Winter’s Tale (Act III, sc. iii) primarily to serve as its clues across. These clues consist of one word in each line and since they were written in or around 1610 solvers should be on the alert for words and meanings now obsolete. Anxious to get on with other work, the Bard never compiled the clues down; so Dogop has supplied normal ones. Shakespeare did however leave a note that the unchecked letters of his across lights form the unchline: ‘GONERIL THE SORRY THRIVER? YES!’—WINTER’S TALE (BARD) and, to avoid pitfalls, solvers are urged to check these letters with those in their completed diagrams.

listener-2046.preamble: The definition part of each clue contains a misprint of one letter only. Thus ‘Hardy’s strange tale’ would lead to LATE (=tardy). With acknowledgments to Ximenes, inventor of this type of clue, who offered some useful criticisms.

listener-2062.preamble: Each clue contains a one-word definition of the light required at the number where it stands. The letters of the solution to each clue are to be reversed to form a new word, which is to be filled in the diagram elsewhere. The number in brackets after each clue refers to the number of letters in both the word clued there and the light required there. Punctuation may mislead.

listener-2302.preamble: Each across clue is a passage from which the printer has omitted a number of consecutive letters. These form the word which answers the clue. On closing the gap, he may have altered punctuation and spacing, but he has not disturbed the order of the remaining letters. E.g. ‘To please the mobile toffs: tea-urn game (7)’ leads to MINARET (‘To please the mob I let off steam in a return game’). In each down clue, the printer has substituted a single false letter for one other, always within the definition part of the clue. E.g. ‘Hardy’s strange tale (4)’ leads to LATE (‘Tardy’s strange tale’). In memory of Afrit and Ximenes, inventors of the across and the down clue-types respectively.

listener-2303.preamble: Eleven of the clues lead to words which are connected in a particular way to the lights to be entered. Solvers may find Brewer’s Dictionary of Phrase and Fable useful, and Chambers’s Twentieth Century Dictionary is recommended. Beware of punctuation.

listener-2310.preamble: There are six words each of 9, 8, 7, 6, 5 and 4 letters. Two of the clues to words of each length are normal, the other four being bluffs: in each of these the subsidiary indications lead to the answer to be entered at the clue-number, but the definition belongs to another word of the same length elsewhere in the diagram. Every word is in Chambers’s Twentieth Century Dictionary, 1972 Edition.

listener-2323.preamble: Certain pairs of words of equal length may be ‘added’ in the following sense to produce two new words: the pair of first, second, third . . . letters of the resulting words shall equal respectively the pair of first, second, third . . . letters of the original pair. For example SAILOR + POSTED = PASTOR + SOILED Each clue is in fact two non-overlapping clues which lead to two words of equal length. These must be ‘added’ and the resulting words entered in the congruent diagrams under the appropriate clue number; either word may occupy either diagram. Chambers’ Twentieth Century Dictionary, 1972 Edition, is recommended. The unchecked letters in the left-hand diagram may be rearranged to form SUCCESS AWAITS AGILE EXPERTS: I GUARD!

listener-2333.preamble: Clues are of the cryptic type but the lights to be entered in the diagram are the phonetic equivalents of the answers as given in Chambers 1972 edition. Where more than one letter is used to indicate a sound (see pages viii and ix) these letters are to be entered in the same square. Punctuation in clues may be misleading.

listener-2458.preamble: Three unidentified lights are in Linear C, the rest are en clair. It would be unfair to suggest that the method used by Michael Ventris to solve Linear B would work.

listener-2463.preamble: Down lights are to be entered normally. These yield one peculiarity in each answer to the Across clues which, when taken together and read correctly, might twice explain the cause.

listener-2544.preamble: Solvers are required to commit a slip of the pen by altering one letter of the answer to each clue when writing it in the diagram. Only at 21 should the substitution affect an unchecked letter. Every word in the completed diagram, as well as every clue’s answer, is in Chambers Twentieth Century Dictionary, 1977 revised edition.
